title: Mollymoss and the Mountain Bells
markdown:
Way up high in the Whispering Peaks, nestled like jewels on the mountainside, were gardens terraced into impossible slopes. Crystal lakes shimmered. Narrow passes, cut like ribbons into sheer rock, led to the villages below. And in one of these terraced homes, a cozy stone dwelling with smoke curling lazily from its chimney, lived a witch named Mollymoss. She wasn’t the cackling pointy-hat kind of witch. Mollymoss wore moss-green robes that smelled faintly of damp earth and thyme, and her hair was the colour of a stormy sky, often escaping its braid to frame a thoughtful face. Her dearest companion, and indeed the most important member of her household, was a ginger cat named Pudding. Pudding was a creature of immense dignity and even more immense naps, his fur the colour of a ripe marmalade, and his purr a rumble that could soothe even the most harried mountain goat.

Mollymoss liked things neat, logical, and quiet. Her shelves were organized by herb potency, her spellbooks dusted weekly, and her days filled with the gentle rustle of drying leaves and the soft murmur of incantations. So when the valley’s ancient warning bells, the ones supposed to ring only for dire emergencies like dragon sightings or truly spectacular awe-inspiring sunsets, began to clang without pause, it quite ruffled her feathers. Clang! Bong! Ding-dong! All day, every day. A relentless jarring symphony. The villagers grumbled so much their beards drooped, their knitting unraveled in frustration, and the baker swore his bread wouldn’t rise out of pure spite.

When she could already picture the elegant logical solution, she sometimes found it hard to understand why everyone else was making such a colossal fuss. She’d tap her chin: honestly, an adjusted pendulum. Why the hand-wringing?

“Pudding, this incessant racket is quite unseemly, wouldn’t you agree?” Stretched on a sunbeam, he blinked large intelligent green eyes; a tail twitch she understood as: indeed, mistress, disruptive to my afternoon repose.

Down in the valley, Mayor Bumblebrook was wringing his hands until they were positively red and aching. The Annual Harvest Festival, a time of joy, music, and exceptionally good apple crumble, was only a fortnight away. If those bells kept ringing their infuriating tune, no one would be in the mood for dancing or feasting. The elders declared it a calamity of the highest order, the young folks worried about missing the opportunity to impress each other, and the mayor felt the weight of a thousand annoyed villagers pressing down on him like a ton of very heavy, very grumpy rocks. If the bells weren’t silenced, the festival would be ruined, and the valley would be steeped in a fog of perpetual grumpiness that would likely last until spring. This was not a situation Mollymoss could ignore, no matter how much she’d rather be tending her delicate moonpetal plants, which bloomed only under the light of the fullest moon. The Harvest Festival was the valley’s last chance for a truly joyful celebration before the long winter.

A sigh that smelled faintly of lavender and a touch of resignation. “Come, Pudding,” she called, picking up her sturdy walking staff, which was carved from a single piece of ancient yew. “We’re going to the valley. And no, you don’t have to wear boots. I find they restrict your essential cat-like grace.” A satisfied purr like tiny thunder; he hopped onto her shoulder.

Off the mountain path: noise and worried faces. Mayor Bumblebrook, portly, waistcoat straining, rushed them, bald head shining. “Mollymoss! Thank the stars! These bells! Driving us to distraction! My prize-winning pumpkin is drooping from sheer agitation!” Hands like startled pigeons, nearly knocking a fruit stall.

Beside him, Wizard Milo, robes shimmering with an alarming number of shifting arcane symbols, magnificent silver beard with a life of its own. “A grave magical disturbance!” Dramatic pose, beard like a wizardly cape. “A counter-spell of immense power! Perhaps a flight of enchanted gargoyles to silence the very air!”

Mollymoss preferred a well-placed cork to a squadron of stone guardians. One eyebrow. “Perhaps we might first ascertain why they are ringing with such gusto.”

Seeing the mayor’s genuine teary-eyed worry, trembling lip, she felt a tiny unexpected pang. She had been so sure it was mechanical, a jiffy. His distress was real. Clamor of voices, rough wool scarves, sour tang of anxiety. A flicker: perhaps Milo’s grand pronouncements weren’t so silly if they made people feel heard. She almost turned back toward the quiet tower. Pudding nudged her cheek. She straightened.

She listened with her whole being to objects and the hum of magic, examining the bell tower. Fingers on ancient weathered mechanisms, vibrations of age and strain. A new crystal-like object nestled near the main bell, pulsing faint internal light.

“It’s this Valley Harmony Crystal. A recent addition, meant to amplify pleasant sounds. Rather overenthusiastic.” Winds, even gentle mountain breezes that usually sang, made it vibrate wildly; the design amplified a thousandfold, inadvertently triggering the bells.

Milo scoffed, a kettle coming to the boil. “A mere crystal? Preposterous! This requires a potent enchantment, a ward of immense power against sonic disruption!”

“Or,” a small smile, “a very small, very precise dampening charm. Pudding, the small silver vial. Star on the stopper.”

A flick of tail, obedient and slightly disdainful of theatrics. The vial glimmered like captured moonlight. Mollymoss prepared a potion of quietude: dew-kissed spiderwebs at dawn, sighs of sleeping dandelions, hushed whispers of a moonbeam.

The charm needed something personal: a small offering of her own essence. Fingers trembled on cool glass. The air, usually humming with her inner calm, went still and expectant. A sigh of pine needles and ancient earth; a single silvery drop of her energy into the potion. It pulsed, pearly. For a fleeting moment the vibrant contented hum within her felt quieter. A tiny piece of serene energy. She felt a little less sharp, a little more attuned to the world’s weary noise.

She poured the shimmering potion onto the crystal. Frantic vibrations ceased. A soft contented glow, then silence. The bells stopped. The silence that followed was so profound it was almost deafening. A collective gasp of relief swept the valley.

Climbing home, the valley at peace below the window. No frantic ringing. Gentle quietude. Mayor Bumblebrook beaming, already organizing festival preparations with renewed vigor. Wizard Milo grumbled about simplicity and lack of dramatic flair, then offered a nod of grudging respect.

Mollymoss sat by her window, sipping a cup of calming chamomile tea. A faint, almost imperceptible mist began to swirl through the fir trees beneath a crumbling ancient tower on a distant peak. Not the dramatic storm-filled mist she’d sometimes conjured for effect, but a soft gentle veil that seemed to whisper of quiet earth and peaceful sky. The quiet within her was not an absence she feared. It was richer, born from watching a pumpkin droop and a mayor’s hands ache, and from one drop that had cost her a little sharpness and bought the valley a fortnight of dancing. Even Wizard Milo, still muttering about gargoyles, helped string lanterns for the festival, which Mollymoss counted as a more useful enchantment than silencing the air. The Harvest Festival, they say, was the best anyone could remember. Pudding, restored to his sunbeam, declined to wear boots to it, and nobody, for once, argued with a cat.
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing mountain fantasy adventure for older children
